claims.source: Notably, the overall proportion of crossover progeny among recombinants identified was increased at all timepoints scored for the brc-1(xoe4) null mutant (Figure 1A), which is similar to the increase in the proportion of ICR assay crossover events we also found in the classical brc-1(tm1145);brd-1(dw1) mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: SCEs are found in only 4.1% of chromatid pairs in a wild type background.
claims.source: While SCEs are found in only 4.1% of chromatid pairs in a wild type background (2/49 chromatid pairs scored, 95% Binomial CI 1.1–13.7%; Almanzar et al., 2021), we detected SCEs at an elevated rate of 19.2% in a brc-1(xoe4) mutant (Figure 1B–C, 5/26 chromatid pairs scored, 95% Binomial CI 8.5–37.9%, Fisher's Exact Test p=0.045).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research and data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: SCEs were detected at an elevated rate of 19.2% in a brc-1(xoe4) mutant.
claims.source: While SCEs are found in only 4.1% of chromatid pairs in a wild type background (2/49 chromatid pairs scored, 95% Binomial CI 1.1–13.7%; Almanzar et al., 2021), we detected SCEs at an elevated rate of 19.2% in a brc-1(xoe4) mutant (Figure 1B–C, 5/26 chromatid pairs scored, 95% Binomial CI 8.5–37.9%, Fisher's Exact Test p=0.045).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 1B-C.

claims.claim: The elevated frequency of SCEs in brc-1 mutants (4.7-fold increase) closely mirrored the relative increase in crossovers as a proportion of all recombinants observed in the brc-1 mutant ICR assay (4.6-fold increase).
claims.source: When we compared the levels of SCEs cytologically identified with the frequency of ICR assay crossovers generated from Mos1-induced DSBs within the interhomolog window, the elevated frequency of SCEs (4.7-fold increase) closely mirrored the relative increase in crossovers as a proportion of all recombinants observed in the brc-1 mutant ICR assay (4.6-fold increase).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by comparison of data from the EdU labeling assay and ICR assay.

claims.claim: brc-1 mutants did not display increased ICR assay recombinants compared to msh-2 mutants.
claims.source: However, msh-2 mutants, which are defective in heteroduplex recognition and rejection (Chakraborty and Alani, 2016), did not display increased ICR assay recombinants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that altered repair template bias does not underpin this effect.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: The ratio of IH assay crossover and noncrossover recombinant progeny within the interhomolog window between wild type and brc-1 mutants was not significantly altered.
claims.source: The ratio of IH assay crossover and noncrossover recombinant progeny within the interhomolog window between wild type and brc-1 mutants was not significantly altered (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, Fisher's Exact Test p=0.515).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: In both the ICR and IH assays performed in brc-1 mutants, progeny exhibited molecular signatures of mutagenic DSB repair at the Mos1 excision site specifically at the 22–34 hr timepoint.
claims.source: In both the ICR and IH assays performed in brc-1 mutants, we identified progeny that exhibited molecular signatures of mutagenic DSB repair at the Mos1 excision site (Figure 1D–E, Figure 1—figure supplement 4). These events were only identified within the 22–34 hr timepoint, which is composed of nuclei in mid pachytene at the time of heat shock.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 1D-E and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: 75% (3/4 mutations) of meiotic mutations in brc-1 IH assay mutant progeny exhibited one or more complementary nucleotides on both ends of the deletion.
claims.source: Of the five GFP+ mutant progeny that we identified in the brc-1 IH assay, four contained single mutations that could be attributed to meiotic repair of the Mos1-excision induced DSB (see Materials and methods), and 75% (3/4 mutations) of these meiotic mutations exhibited one or more complementary nucleotides on both ends of the deletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by sequencing data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claims.claim: The single mutant identified among brc-1 ICR assay GFP+ progeny displayed a duplication joined at a position sharing microhomology.
claims.source: Further, the single mutant identified among brc-1 ICR assay GFP+ progeny displayed a particularly striking duplication joined at a position sharing microhomology (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by sequencing data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: Regions of microhomology present on either end of small (<50 bp) deletions and templated insertions are characteristic of theta-mediated end joining (TMEJ).
claims.source: Regions of microhomology present on either end of small (<50 bp) deletions and templated insertions are characteristic of theta-mediated end joining (TMEJ) (van Schendel et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: The rate of TMEJ-mediated germline mutagenesis is elevated in brc-1 mutants.
claims.source: A previous study demonstrated that the rate of TMEJ-mediated germline mutagenesis is elevated in brc-1 mutants (Kamp et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: The frequency of GFP+ progeny in the ICR assay was elevated at all timepoints scored in smc-5(ok2421) null mutants.
claims.source: Similar to brc-1 mutants, we found that the frequency of GFP+ progeny in the ICR assay was elevated at all timepoints scored in smc-5(ok2421) null mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and was not reduced relative to wild type in null smc-6(ok3294) mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The frequency of crossover recombinants in smc-5 mutants was significantly elevated within the interhomolog window overall in the ICR assay.
claims.source: While the proportion of crossovers was not significantly different than wild-type within the individual 12 hr timepoints we scored (Figure 2A), the frequency of crossover recombinants in smc-5 mutants was significantly elevated within the interhomolog window overall (Figure 2B, Fisher's Exact Test p=0.037).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: SCEs were identified in 35.7% of scored chromatid pairs in smc-5(ok2421) mutants.
claims.source: Despite these challenges, we identified SCEs in 35.7% of scored chromatid pairs (Figure 2C–D, 5/14 chromatid pairs scored, 95% Binomial CI 16.3–61.2%, Fisher's Exact Test p=0.004) as compared to only 4.1% of wild type chromatid pairs (2/49 chromatid pairs scored, 95% Binomial CI 1.1–13.7%) (Almanzar et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 2C-D.

claims.claim: Among all sequenced ICR and IH assay GFP+ and non-Unc progeny isolated in smc-5 mutants, only one mutagenic DSB repair event was identified at the 22–34 hr timepoint of the IH assay.
claims.source: Among all sequenced ICR and IH assay GFP+ and non-Unc progeny isolated in smc-5 mutants, we identified only one mutagenic DSB repair event at the 22–34 hr timepoint of the IH assay (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplements 1A and 2A).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplements 1A and 2A.

claims.claim: The frequency of smc-5 non-Unc mutants detected at the 22-34 hr timepoint (1.32% of all sequenced non-Unc progeny) is lower than the frequency observed in brc-1 mutants.
claims.source: Moreover, the frequency of smc-5 non-Unc mutants that we detected at this timepoint (1.32% of all sequenced non-Unc progeny, 95% Binomial CI 0.2–7.1%) is lower than the frequency observed in brc-1 mutants (Fisher's Exact Test p=0.015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by comparison of sequencing data from smc-5 and brc-1 mutants.

claims.claim: Large structural variations are a primary class of mutations that arise in SMC-5/6 deficient germlines.
claims.source: Profiling of meiotic mutagenic DNA repair events in smc-6 mutants has indicated that large structural variations are a primary class of mutations that arise in SMC-5/6 deficient germlines (Volkova et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: 74.2% of ICR assay noncrossover conversion tracts within the interhomolog window in wild type are 'short' (tracts with a sequence conversion only at the most proximal polymorphism 12 bp downstream from the site of Mos1 excision).
claims.source: In a wild type context, 74.2% of ICR assay noncrossover conversion tracts within the interhomolog window are 'short', which we define as tracts with a sequence conversion only at the most proximal polymorphism 12 bp downstream from the site of Mos1 excision (Figure 3A and C, wild type 74.2% short tracts 95% CI 62.6–83.3%).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 3A and C.

claims.claim: 96.6% of brc-1 noncrossover tracts during the interhomolog window were 'short'.
claims.source: In contrast, 96.6% of brc-1 noncrossover tracts during the interhomolog window were 'short' (brc-1 interhomolog window 96.6% short tracts 95% CI 82.8–99.4%, Fisher's Exact Test p=0.010).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 3A and C.

claims.claim: The proportion of 'short' crossover tracts was not altered by brc-1 mutation within the interhomolog window.
claims.source: We found that the proportion of 'short' crossover tracts was not altered by brc-1 mutation within the interhomolog window (Figure 3B and D, wild type 80.0% short tracts 95% CI 62.7–90.5%; brc-1 74.1% short tracts 95% CI 61.1–83.9%, Fisher's Exact Test P=1.000) nor within the non-interhomolog window (Figure 3B and D, wild type 55.6% short tracts 95% CI 37.3–72.4%; brc-1 68.8% short tracts 95% CI 44.4–58.8%, Fisher's Exact Test p=0.657).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 3B and D.

claims.claim: ICR assay noncrossover conversion tracts in smc-5 mutants exhibited a similar proportion of 'short' tracts to wild type in both the interhomolog and non-interhomolog windows.
claims.source: We found that ICR assay noncrossover conversion tracts in smc-5 mutants exhibited a similar proportion of 'short' tracts to wild type in both the interhomolog (Figure 3A and C, wild type 74.2% short tracts 95% CI 62.6–83.3%; smc-5 82.6% short tracts 95% CI 69.3–90.9%, Fisher's Exact Test p=0.360) and non-interhomolog windows (Figure 3A and C, wild type 72.7% short tracts 95% CI 51.8–86.8%; smc-5 70% short tracts 95% CI 39.7–89.2%).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 3A and C.

claims.claim: There is no significant difference in the proportion of short and long crossover tracts in smc-5 mutants compared to wild type in either the interhomolog or non-interhomolog windows.
claims.source: When we compared the proportion of 'short' smc-5 ICR assay crossover tracts to wild type, we similarly observed that there is no significant difference in the proportion of short and long crossover tracts in either the interhomolog (Figure 3B and D, wild type 80.0% short tracts 95% CI 62.7–90.5%; smc-5 57.9% short tracts 95% CI 36.3—76.9%, Fisher's Exact Test p=1.000) or non-interhomolog windows (Figure 3B and D, wild type 55.6% short tracts 95% CI 37.3–72.4%; smc-5 62.5% short tracts 95% CI 30.6–86.3%, Fisher's Exact Test p=1.000).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 3B and D.

claims.claim: Multiple instances of heteroduplex DNA were noted in wild type, brc-1, and smc-5 ICR assay conversion tracts.
claims.source: In our wild type, brc-1, and smc-5 ICR assay conversion tracts, we additionally noted multiple instances of heteroduplex DNA in our sequencing (Figure 3A and B asterisks).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: The proportion of ICR assay crossover recombinants in smc-5::AID*;brc-1 mutants was elevated relative to wild type at both the 22–34 hr and 46–58 hr timepoints within the interhomolog window but was indistinguishable from brc-1 single mutants at all timepoints assayed.
claims.source: Further, the proportion of ICR assay crossover recombinants in smc-5::AID*;brc-1 mutants was elevated relative to wild type at both the 22–34 hr and 46–58 hr timepoints within the interhomolog window but was indistinguishable from brc-1 single mutants at all timepoints assayed (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The increased number of RAD-51 foci per nucleus in smc-5 mutants was suppressed when brc-1 was also mutated.
claims.source: Strikingly, we observed that the increased number of RAD-51 foci per nucleus in smc-5 mutants was suppressed when brc-1 was also mutated (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: BRC-1 is required to load and/or maintain RAD-51 localization to DSBs at mid/late pachytene when interhomolog recombination is perturbed.
claims.source: BRC-1 is required to load and/or maintain RAD-51 localization to DSBs at mid/late pachytene when interhomolog recombination is perturbed (Li et al., 2018; Janisiw et al., 2018) as well as following induction of exogenous DSBs from sources such as ionizing radiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C; Li et al., 2018; Janisiw et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research and data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 4C.

claims.claim: Loss of smc-5 conveys a greater sensitivity to exogenous DNA damage than loss of brc-1 across all irradiation doses and timepoints.
claims.source: Across all irradiation doses and timepoints, we note that loss of smc-5 conveys a greater sensitivity to exogenous DNA damage than loss of brc-1 (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), emphasizing that the SMC-5/6 complex prevents catastrophic defects following exogenous DNA damage induction.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: The sensitivity of brc-1 mutants was greater in the non-interhomolog window at high doses of irradiation.
claims.source: The sensitivity of brc-1 mutants was greater in the non-interhomolog window at high doses of irradiation (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), suggesting that nuclei in late pachytene become more dependent upon BRC-1 to efficiently resolve DNA damage.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: At 2500 Rad of ionizing radiation, the smc-5;brc-1 double mutant and smc-5 single mutant gamma estimates overlap in the interhomolog window.
claims.source: In the interhomolog window, the smc-5;brc-1 double mutant and smc-5 single mutant gamma estimates overlap, indicating that loss of BRC-1 does not alter smc-5 mutant sensitivity at this timepoint (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: A striking suppression of sensitivity to exogenous DSBs was observed in smc-5;brc-1 double mutants as compared to smc-5 single mutants in the non-interhomolog window at 2500 Rads.
claims.source: In the non-interhomolog window, however, we observed a striking suppression of sensitivity to exogenous DSBs in smc-5;brc-1 double mutants as compared to smc-5 single mutants (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Synthetic suppression of radiation-induced brood lethality is recapitulated across meiotic prophase I at 5000 Rads of ionizing radiation in smc-5;brc-1 double mutants.
claims.source: This synthetic suppression of sensitivity is recapitulated across meiotic prophase I at 5000 Rads of ionizing radiation in smc-5;brc-1 double mutants (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: lig-4 mutation did not fully suppress the synthetic radiation resilience of smc-5;brc-1 mutants.
claims.source: lig-4 mutation did not fully suppress the synthetic radiation resilience of smc-5;brc-1 mutants, suggesting that NHEJ is not a primary mechanism of DNA repair in meiotic nuclei when both SMC-5/6 and BRC-1 are lost.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data from irradiation experiments.

claims.claim: Loss of POLQ-1 caused dramatic sensitization of smc-5;brc-1 mutants to ionizing radiation at 2500 Rads.
claims.source: However, we observed a striking effect in smc-5;brc-1;polq-1 mutants; even at the moderate dose of 2500 Rads, loss of POLQ-1 caused dramatic sensitization of smc-5;brc-1 mutants to ionizing radiation (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: smc-5;brc-1;polq-1 mutants were nearly sterile following ionizing radiation treatment in the non-interhomolog window regardless of irradiation dose.
claims.source: This effect was particularly strong in the non-interhomolog window, where smc-5;brc-1;polq-1 mutants were nearly sterile following ionizing radiation treatment regardless of irradiation dose (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: The increased radiation sensitivity of smc-5;brc-1;polq-1 within the non-interhomolog window was not rescued by mating to unirradiated wild type males.
claims.source: However, the increased radiation sensitivity of smc-5;brc-1;polq-1 within the non-interhomolog window was not rescued by mating (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–B).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-B.

claims.claim: BRC-1 localizes as a nuclear haze in the premeiotic tip through early pachytene and becomes associated with the synaptonemal complex during the progression of pachytene in wild-type germlines.
claims.source: Similar to previous studies (Li et al., 2018; Janisiw et al., 2018), we observed that BRC-1 localizes as a nuclear haze in the premeiotic tip through early pachytene and becomes associated with the synaptonemal complex during the progression of pachytene in wild-type germlines (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: In late pachytene, BRC-1 relocates to the short arms of the bivalents, where it can be visualized at diplotene as short tracks on the compacted chromosome arms.
claims.source: In late pachytene, BRC-1 relocates to the short arms of the bivalents, where it can be visualized at diplotene as short tracks on the compacted chromosome arms (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: In smc-5 mutants, GFP::BRC-1 formed bright foci in the premeiotic tip.
claims.source: When we examined smc-5 mutants, the general pattern of GFP::BRC-1 localization across meiotic prophase was similar to wild type, except in the premeiotic tip where GFP::BRC-1 formed bright foci (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The bright GFP::BRC-1 foci in the pre-meiotic tip of smc-5 mutants likely mark BRC-1 localization to collapsed replication forks.
claims.source: Given that BRD-1, the obligate heterodimeric partner of BRC-1, was found to form a similar localization in smc-5 mutants (Wolters et al., 2014), the bright GFP::BRC-1 foci in the pre-meiotic tip likely mark BRC-1 localization to collapsed replication forks (Bickel et al., 2010; Wolters et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by inference from prior research on BRD-1 localization and citations.

claims.claim: The general pattern of GFP::BRC-1 localization was not altered following irradiation in both wild type and smc-5 mutants.
claims.source: We found that the general pattern of GFP::BRC-1 localization was not altered following irradiation in both wild type and smc-5 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: SMC-5 staining in early and mid-pachytene was primarily localized to the chromosome axis, marked with HTP-3.
claims.source: Notably, we found that SMC-5 staining in early and mid-pachytene was primarily localized to the chromosome axis, marked with HTP-3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: SMC-5 localization pattern was altered in the transition to the diplotene stage, when SMC-5 localizes to the chromatin on the compacting bivalent chromosomes.
claims.source: This localization pattern was altered in the transition to the diplotene stage, when we observed that SMC-5 localizes to the chromatin on the compacting bivalent chromosomes, matching previous analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 5; Bickel et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 5 and a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: The pattern of SMC-5 localization was not disrupted in a brc-1 mutant.
claims.source: The pattern of SMC-5 localization was not disrupted in a brc-1 mutant, and similarly was not altered following exposure to 5000 Rads of ionizing radiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: BRC-1 regulates mechanisms of intersister/intrachromatid recombination that determine noncrossover gene conversion tract length (but not crossover tract length) during meiotic prophase I.
claims.source: Taken together, these results support a model in which BRC-1 regulates mechanisms of intersister/intrachromatid recombination that determine noncrossover gene conversion tract length (but not crossover tract length) during meiotic prophase I (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by conversion tract analysis data showing that brc-1 mutants have shorter noncrossover tracts but normal crossover tracts.

claims.claim: Some functions of BRC-1 act upstream of SMC-5/6 to promote recombination and inhibit error-prone DSB repair.
claims.source: These results are consistent with a model in which some functions of BRC-1 act upstream of SMC-5/6 to promote recombination and inhibit error-prone DSB repair, while SMC-5/6 acts downstream of BRC-1 to regulate the formation or resolution of recombination intermediates.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by genetic interaction data and RAD-51 foci analysis.

claims.claim: SMC-5/6 acts downstream of BRC-1 to regulate the formation or resolution of recombination intermediates.
claims.source: These results are consistent with a model in which some functions of BRC-1 act upstream of SMC-5/6 to promote recombination and inhibit error-prone DSB repair, while SMC-5/6 acts downstream of BRC-1 to regulate the formation or resolution of recombination intermediates.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by genetic interaction data and conversion tract analysis.

claims.claim: BRCA1 is thought to regulate many early steps in recombination including DSB resection, strand invasion, and D-loop formation in other model systems.
claims.source: BRCA1 is thought to regulate many early steps in recombination including DSB resection, strand invasion, and D-loop formation in other model systems (Kamp et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2008; Cruz-García et al., 2014; Chandramouly et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Human BRCA1 promotes strand invasion and D-loop formation.
claims.source: Human BRCA1 promotes strand invasion and D-loop formation (Zhao et al., 2017), which may influence the efficiency of strand extension.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: BRCA1 regulates DSB resection.
claims.source: Previous studies have also suggested that BRCA1/BRC-1 regulates DSB resection (Chen et al., 2008; Cruz-García et al., 2014), and we propose that this function better accounts for our observed increase in intersister crossovers in the brc-1 null mutant.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Long range resection is not required for the efficient formation of joint molecules.
claims.source: While sufficient resection may be critical in resolving SDSA noncrossovers, long range resection is not required for the efficient formation of joint molecules (Zakharyevich et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Polymerase θ helicase activity is sufficient to remove recombinases from single-stranded DNA to promote end-joining repair.
claims.source: Polymerase θ helicase activity is also sufficient to remove recombinases from single-stranded DNA to promote end-joining repair (Schaub et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: In budding yeast, Smc5/6 prevents the accumulation of toxic interchromosomal attachments and recombination intermediates.
claims.source: In budding yeast, Smc5/6 prevents the accumulation of toxic interchromosomal attachments and recombination intermediates (Bonner et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2009; Peng et al., 2018; Xaver et al., 2013; Lilienthal et al., 2013; Copsey et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Double mutants for smc-5 and the BLM helicase homolog him-6 are sterile and display chromatin bridges indicative of persistent interchromosomal attachments.
claims.source: Prior evidence in C. elegans suggests that some of these functions are likely conserved, as double mutants for smc-5 and the BLM helicase homolog him-6 are sterile and display chromatin bridges indicative of persistent interchromosomal attachments (Hong et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Both SMC-5 and HIM-6 repress intersister crossovers.
claims.source: A previous study (Almanzar et al., 2021) and the data we present here reveal that both SMC-5 and HIM-6 repress intersister crossovers.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research and data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: A core function of BLM helicase is in antagonism of joint molecule formation and promotion of noncrossover recombination.
claims.source: Although BLM is known to play multiple roles in regulating recombination, a core function of this helicase is in antagonism of joint molecule formation and promotion of noncrossover recombination (Schvarzstein et al., 2014; McVey et al., 2004; Weinert and Rio, 2007).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: SMC5/6 is capable of DNA loop-extrusion.
claims.source: Recent work has shown that SMC5/6 is capable of DNA loop-extrusion, indicating a function by which the complex may organize chromatin to facilitate efficient DSB repair (Pradhan et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Specific subunits of SMC-5/6 exhibit enzymatic function, such as the E3 SUMO ligase Nse2/Mms21.
claims.source: Specific subunits of SMC-5/6 also exhibit enzymatic function, such as the E3 SUMO ligase Nse2/Mms21 (Andrews et al., 2005), suggesting that SMC-5/6 may act to post-translationally modify target proteins to regulate DNA repair.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: In mitotic human cell culture, Polθ is phosphorylated and activated in specific stages of mitosis by polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1).
claims.source: In mitotic human cell culture, Polθ is phosphorylated and activated in specific stages of mitosis by polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1; Gelot et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: The C. elegans meiotic polo-like kinase ortholog PLK-2 acts in mid-late pachytene to antagonize CHK-2 activity, thereby promoting interhomolog crossover designation and halting DSB induction.
claims.source: The C. elegans meiotic polo-like kinase ortholog PLK-2 acts in mid-late pachytene to antagonize CHK-2 activity, thereby promoting interhomolog crossover designation and halting DSB induction (Zhang et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: C. elegans meiotic POLQ-1 may be activated in late stages of meiotic prophase I by PLK-2 analogously to mitotic human Polθ activation by PLK1.
claims.source: We raise the hypothesis that C. elegans meiotic POLQ-1 may be activated in late stages of meiotic prophase I by PLK-2 analogously to mitotic human Polθ activation by PLK1.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on inference from prior research on PLK1 and PLK-2.

claims.claim: Both brc-1 and smc-5 mutant oocytes exhibit greater sensitivity to exogenous DNA damage in late stages of prophase I.
claims.source: Our irradiation experiments revealed that both brc-1 and smc-5 mutant oocytes exhibit greater sensitivity to exogenous DNA damage in late stages of prophase I, suggesting that cellular requirements for efficacious DSB repair change during the transition to late pachytene.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by irradiation experiment data.

claims.claim: BRC-1 protein localization changes during the mid-late pachytene stage.
claims.source: Moreover, during the mid-late pachytene stage, several changes regarding BRC-1 occur: (1) BRC-1 protein localization changes; and, (2) BRC-1 is required to load (and/or stabilize) RAD-51 filaments (Li et al., 2018; Janisiw et al., 2018; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: polq-1 is expressed throughout meiotic prophase I.
claims.source: Spatiotemporal transcriptomic analysis has shown that polq-1 is expressed throughout meiotic prophase I (Tzur et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: BRC-1 independent mechanisms may repress TMEJ in early/mid pachytene.

claims.claim: The engagement of error-prone and recombination DSB repair pathways are differentially regulated during the course of C. elegans meiotic prophase I.
claims.source: Taken together, our study reveals that the engagement of error-prone and recombination DSB repair pathways are differentially regulated during the course of C. elegans meiotic prophase I.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data showing stage-specific mutagenic repair and differential sensitivity to irradiation.

claims.source: Instead, we propose that BRC-1 and SMC-5/6 exert sequential roles in regulation of DSB repair. A similar model was proposed by Hong et al., 2016 which postulated that early recombination defects in brc-1 mutants may alleviate the toxic recombination intermediates formed in smc-5;him-6 double mutants.

results.result: BRC-1 represses intersister crossover recombination during C. elegans meiosis. The proportion of crossover recombinants in the ICR assay was elevated in brc-1 mutants at all timepoints, and sister chromatid exchanges (SCEs) were detected at 19.2% in brc-1 mutants compared to 4.1% in wild type, representing a 4.7-fold increase that closely mirrors the 4.6-fold increase in ICR assay crossovers.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C29-C32 provide converging evidence from both genetic (ICR assay) and cytological (EdU labeling) approaches showing elevated intersister crossovers in brc-1 mutants. The concordance between the 4.7-fold increase in SCEs and 4.6-fold increase in ICR crossovers strengthens the conclusion. Statistical significance is demonstrated (p=0.045 for SCEs, p<0.05 for multiple ICR timepoints).

results.result: BRC-1 regulates intersister/intrachromatid noncrossover conversion tract length but not crossover tract length. In brc-1 mutants, 96.6% of noncrossover tracts were 'short' (≤12 bp) compared to 74.2% in wild type (p=0.010), while crossover tract lengths were not significantly altered.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C46-C48, and C72 demonstrate a specific effect of BRC-1 on noncrossover tract length with appropriate statistical testing (Fisher's Exact Test p=0.010). The differential effect on noncrossovers versus crossovers (C48, p=1.000) supports the specificity of this function. The data directly support the mechanistic model proposed in C72.

results.result: BRC-1 specifically inhibits error-prone repair of DSBs induced at mid-pachytene. Mutagenic repair events with TMEJ signatures were identified exclusively at the 22-34 hr timepoint (mid-pachytene) in both ICR and IH assays in brc-1 mutants, with 75% of mutations exhibiting microhomology characteristic of TMEJ.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C35-C39 demonstrate stage-specific mutagenic repair in brc-1 mutants with molecular signatures consistent with TMEJ (microhomology at deletion junctions). The temporal specificity (only at 22-34 hr) is well-documented across two independent assays. The connection to TMEJ is supported by both molecular signatures (C36-C38) and prior literature (C39).

results.result: BRC-1 is required for RAD-51 localization to DSBs in smc-5 mutants. The elevated RAD-51 foci observed in smc-5 mutants were suppressed in smc-5;brc-1 double mutants, indicating that BRC-1 promotes recombinase loading even when recombination is defective.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C53-C54, and C95 demonstrate genetic suppression of the smc-5 RAD-51 phenotype by brc-1 mutation with quantitative imaging data (Figure 4B). The interpretation is consistent with prior work showing BRC-1's role in RAD-51 loading (C54). Statistical significance is demonstrated across multiple meiotic stages with appropriate corrections for multiple comparisons.

results.result: BRC-1 enhances DSB repair defects in smc-5 mutants by repressing TMEJ. Loss of POLQ-1 caused dramatic sensitization of smc-5;brc-1 double mutants to ionizing radiation (2500 Rads), with near sterility in the non-interhomolog window, while lig-4 mutation did not fully suppress radiation resilience.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C60-C63 demonstrate that TMEJ (via POLQ-1) is essential for viability in smc-5;brc-1 mutants following DNA damage, while NHEJ (via LIG-4) is not. The dramatic effect of polq-1 mutation is well-documented with appropriate controls including mating experiments (C63) to exclude sperm-specific effects. The Bayesian statistical modeling approach appropriately accounts for baseline fertility differences.

results.result: SMC-5 represses intersister crossover recombination during C. elegans meiosis. The frequency of crossover recombinants in smc-5 mutants was significantly elevated in the interhomolog window (p=0.037), and SCEs were detected in 35.7% of chromatid pairs in smc-5 mutants compared to 4.1% in wild type (p=0.004).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C40-C42, and C82 provide evidence from both ICR assay and EdU labeling showing elevated intersister crossovers in smc-5 mutants. However, the EdU data has limitations due to chromosome morphology issues in smc-5 mutants (small sample size: 5/14 pairs), which the authors acknowledge. The ICR assay data is more robust but shows significance only when timepoints are pooled (C41), not at individual timepoints.

results.result: SMC-5 does not regulate the extent of homolog-independent gene conversion. ICR assay conversion tracts in smc-5 mutants showed similar proportions of 'short' tracts to wild type for both noncrossovers (p=0.360) and crossovers (p=1.000).
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 demonstrate no significant effect of smc-5 mutation on conversion tract length with appropriate statistical testing. This negative result is important for distinguishing SMC-5 function from BRC-1 function and is adequately powered based on sample sizes presented in Figure 3.

results.result: BRC-1 and SMC-5 exhibit stage-specific and differential sensitivities to exogenous DNA damage during meiotic prophase I. Loss of smc-5 confers greater sensitivity than loss of brc-1 across all doses and timepoints, while brc-1 mutants show greater sensitivity in late pachytene at high doses. In the non-interhomolog window, smc-5;brc-1 double mutants show striking suppression of radiation sensitivity compared to smc-5 single mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 and C89 demonstrate complex genetic interactions with appropriate Bayesian statistical modeling to account for baseline fertility differences. The stage-specific effects are well-documented with credible interval analysis. However, the interpretation relies heavily on the gamma metric, which is a derived parameter from the Beta-Binomial model. The biological interpretation of synthetic suppression is sound but mechanistically complex.

results.result: BRC-1 is not required for efficient interhomolog recombination. The ratio of IH assay crossover and noncrossover recombinants was not significantly altered in brc-1 mutants (p=0.515), consistent with prior reports that interhomolog crossover formation is largely unaffected by brc-1 mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C34 and C26 demonstrate that BRC-1 does not have a major role in interhomolog recombination outcomes, which is important for distinguishing its function in intersister versus interhomolog repair. The data is supported by appropriate statistical testing and is consistent with prior literature (C26).

results.result: BRC-1 and SMC-5/6 exert sequential roles in DSB repair regulation, with BRC-1 acting upstream to promote recombination and inhibit error-prone repair, while SMC-5/6 acts downstream to regulate recombination intermediate formation or resolution. Depletion of SMC-5 in brc-1 mutants did not enhance intersister crossover defects beyond brc-1 single mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C52, C73-C74, C94, C99-C100 propose a sequential model based on genetic interaction data. The ICR assay data in smc-5::AID;brc-1 mutants (C52) shows epistasis, supporting the model. However, this is primarily an interpretive framework synthesizing multiple observations rather than direct mechanistic evidence. The model is consistent with all presented data but alternative models are not rigorously excluded.

results.result: Altered repair template bias does not underpin increased recombinants in brc-1 mutants. msh-2 mutants, which are defective in heteroduplex recognition and rejection, did not display increased ICR assay recombinants.
results.evaluation: Claim C33 provides a negative control experiment to test an alternative hypothesis for increased recombinants in brc-1 mutants. The msh-2 data effectively rules out heteroduplex rejection as the mechanism, though the authors acknowledge they cannot definitively explain the increased recombinant frequency in brc-1 ICR assays.

results.result: SMC-5 mutants show lower frequency of detectable mutagenic repair at mid-pachytene compared to brc-1 mutants. Only one mutagenic event was identified in smc-5 mutants (1.32% of sequenced progeny) compared to higher frequencies in brc-1 mutants (p=0.015), though large structural variations may escape detection in the assays used.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45 document a difference in detectable mutagenic repair between smc-5 and brc-1 mutants with appropriate statistical comparison. The authors appropriately acknowledge detection limitations (C45) - large structural variations characteristic of SMC-5/6 deficiency would disrupt GFP/unc-5 coding sequences and escape detection. This is an important caveat that limits interpretation.

results.result: Heteroduplex DNA was observed in wild type, brc-1, and smc-5 ICR assay conversion tracts, suggesting that mismatch repair occasionally fails to resolve heteroduplex DNA during C. elegans meiotic DSB repair.
results.evaluation: Claim C51 reports an observation of heteroduplex DNA across genotypes. This is a descriptive finding with appropriate confirmation (samples were re-sequenced). However, the frequency and biological significance are not quantified, limiting interpretation. This is a minor observational result rather than a central finding.

results.result: BRC-1 localization is independent of SMC-5/6. BRC-1 localizes as a nuclear haze in early prophase, associates with the synaptonemal complex during pachytene progression, and relocates to bivalent short arms in late pachytene. In smc-5 mutants, BRC-1 forms bright foci in the premeiotic tip (likely marking collapsed replication forks) but otherwise shows normal localization patterns that are not altered by irradiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 document BRC-1 localization patterns with immunofluorescence data. The interpretation of bright foci in smc-5 mutants as collapsed replication forks (C67) is inference based on prior work with BRD-1, not direct evidence. The conclusion that BRC-1 localization is independent of SMC-5/6 is supported, though functional independence is not directly tested by localization alone.

results.result: SMC-5 localization is independent of BRC-1. SMC-5 localizes primarily to the chromosome axis in early/mid-pachytene and relocates to chromatin on compacting bivalents at diplotene. This pattern is not disrupted in brc-1 mutants or following irradiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 document SMC-5 localization patterns with immunofluorescence data consistent with prior work (C70). The conclusion that SMC-5 localization is independent of BRC-1 is supported by the data, though as with BRC-1, localization independence does not necessarily indicate functional independence.

results.result: Background and prior work establishing the context for meiotic DSB repair in C. elegans. This includes established principles of meiosis, DSB repair pathways, prior characterization of BRC-1 and SMC-5/6 functions, and genetic interactions between these proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C28 represent background knowledge and prior work appropriately cited from the literature. These establish the scientific context but are not novel findings of this study. The citations appear appropriate and the characterizations are consistent with established knowledge in the field.

results.result: Discussion of mechanistic models and prior work from other systems. This includes BRCA1 functions in DSB resection and strand invasion, SMC5/6 functions in preventing toxic recombination intermediates, BLM helicase functions, and potential regulatory mechanisms involving PLK kinases and POLQ-1.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C98 (selected) represent discussion of mechanisms and prior work from other model systems used to interpret the current findings. These are appropriately cited and provide context for mechanistic interpretation, but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Hypotheses for future investigation. The authors propose that C. elegans POLQ-1 may be activated in late prophase I by PLK-2 (analogous to human Polθ activation by PLK1), and that BRC-1-independent mechanisms may repress TMEJ in early/mid pachytene.
results.evaluation: Claims C88 and C92 are explicitly stated as hypotheses or possibilities raised by the data, not as supported conclusions. C88 is speculative based on analogy to other systems. C92 is inferred from the observation that mutagenic repair occurs only at mid-pachytene despite polq-1 expression throughout prophase I. These represent reasonable directions for future work but lack direct experimental support.

results.result: Synthesis and interpretation of temporal regulation of DSB repair pathways. The authors conclude that error-prone and recombination DSB repair pathways are differentially regulated during meiotic prophase I, and that many DSBs in smc-5;brc-1 mutants are likely repaired by recombination-independent pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C93 and C97 represent synthetic conclusions drawn from multiple lines of evidence presented in the study. C93 is well-supported by the stage-specific mutagenic repair data and differential radiation sensitivity. C97 is inference from the suppression of RAD-51 foci and dependence on POLQ-1, which is reasonable but indirect.
